items.signature: 80 of 2,400 members, 18 hike weekly -> 540; traps 432 (18 as percent), 1,860 (complement), 2,382 (subtract)
items.stem: A hiking club has 2,400 members. A random sample of 80 members was selected, and 18 of the members in the sample said they hike every week during the winter. Based on the sample, which of the following is the best estimate of the number of club members who hike every week during the winter?

choices.feedback: This treats 18 as a percent: $0.18 \times 2{,}400 = 432$. But 18 is a count out of 80 members, which is $22.5\%$.
This estimates the members who do NOT hike every week: $\frac{62}{80} \times 2{,}400$.
This subtracts 18 from 2,400. A sample count must be scaled up, not subtracted.

solution.key_idea: A random sample mirrors its population, so the fraction in the sample is the best estimate of the fraction in the whole club.
solution.steps:
The question asks for the number of ALL club members who hike every week.
sample fraction $= \frac{18}{80}$ (18 out of the 80 sampled members)
estimate $= \frac{18}{80} \times 2{,}400$ (apply the same fraction to the whole club)
$= 18 \times 30 = 540$ ($2{,}400 \div 80 = 30$)
About 540 of the 2,400 members hike every week in winter, the same share as 18 out of 80.
solution.be_careful: 18 is a count, not a percent. Turn it into a fraction of the 80 sampled members first.
solution.another_way: Each sampled member stands for $\frac{2{,}400}{80} = 30$ members, so $18 \times 30 = 540$.

items.signature: mean commute 23.4, MOE 1.8: plausible population mean 21.6 to 25.2; traps individuals, exact, one-sided
items.stem: A random sample of employees at a large hospital was asked how long their commute to work takes. Based on the sample, the mean commute time of all employees at the hospital is estimated to be 23.4 minutes, with an associated margin of error of 1.8 minutes. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

choices.text: It is plausible that every employee at the hospital has a commute time between 21.6 and 25.2 minutes.
choices.feedback: The interval is about the MEAN commute time, not about each employee. Individual commutes can be much shorter or longer.

choices.text: The mean commute time of all employees at the hospital is exactly 23.4 minutes, since the sample was random.
choices.feedback: 23.4 is only an estimate. A random sample does not give the exact population mean.

choices.text: It is plausible that the mean commute time of all employees at the hospital is between 21.6 and 25.2 minutes.
It is plausible that the mean commute time of all employees at the hospital is between 23.4 and 25.2 minutes.
choices.feedback: The margin of error goes both ways: subtract 1.8 as well as add it.

solution.key_idea: Estimate $\pm$ margin of error gives the plausible values of the POPULATION mean, not of individual values.
solution.steps:
The question asks what the estimate and margin of error let us say.
lower end: $23.4 - 1.8 = 21.6$ (subtract the margin)
upper end: $23.4 + 1.8 = 25.2$ (add the margin)
So the plausible values for the mean commute time of all hospital employees run from 21.6 to 25.2 minutes.
solution.be_careful: The interval describes the population mean, not every person.
solution.another_way: Eliminate: “exactly” is too strong, “every employee” is about individuals, and the one-sided interval forgets the minus side.

items.signature: plausible proportion 0.37 to 0.53 -> MOE .08; common wrong .16 width, .45 center
items.stem: Based on a random sample of households in a county, a researcher concluded that the proportion of all households in the county that have a vegetable garden is plausibly between 0.37 and 0.53. This range is the estimate plus or minus the margin of error. What is the margin of error?

common_wrong.feedback: 0.16 is the whole width of the range. The margin of error is half of the width, since it is added and subtracted.
0.45 is the estimate (the center), not the margin of error.

solution.key_idea: The margin of error is the distance from the estimate to either end, so it is half the width of the range.
solution.steps:
The question asks for the margin of error.
width $= 0.53 - 0.37 = 0.16$ (distance from end to end)
margin of error $= \frac{0.16}{2} = 0.08$ (the margin is added on one side and subtracted on the other)
So the range is the estimate, 0.45, plus or minus 0.08.
solution.check: The estimate is $\frac{0.37 + 0.53}{2} = 0.45$, and $0.45 \pm 0.08$ gives 0.37 and 0.53 ✓
solution.be_careful: The width counts the margin twice.
solution.another_way: Find the center 0.45 first; the margin is $0.53 - 0.45 = 0.08$.

highest: $6.2 + 0.4 = 6.6$ (add the margin)
$5.8 \le 6.5 \le 6.6$ (only 6.5 is inside)

solution.be_careful: Values close to the estimate are not automatically plausible; check them against both ends.
solution.another_way: A value is plausible when its distance from 6.2 is at most 0.4: $|6.5 - 6.2| = 0.3$.

items.stem: A town has 18,000 residents. Based on a random sample of residents, it is estimated that 30% of all residents ride a bicycle at least once a week, with an associated margin of error of 4%. Which of the following is a plausible value for the number of residents of the town who ride a bicycle at least once a week?

choices.feedback: 4,500 is 25% of 18,000, below the lowest plausible percent, 26%.
6,300 is 35% of 18,000, above the highest plausible percent, 34%.
12,600 is 70% of 18,000, the residents who do NOT ride weekly.

solution.key_idea: Turn the plausible range of percents into a plausible range of counts by taking each end of the range of 18,000.
solution.steps:
The question asks which count is plausible.
percents: $30\% - 4\% = 26\%$ to $30\% + 4\% = 34\%$ (estimate $\pm$ margin)
$0.26 \times 18{,}000 = 4{,}680$ (lowest count)
$0.34 \times 18{,}000 = 6{,}120$ (highest count)
$4{,}680 \le 5{,}900 \le 6{,}120$ (only 5,900 fits)
solution.be_careful: Compare counts with counts, or percents with percents, never a count with a percent.
solution.another_way: Convert each choice to a percent of 18,000: 25%, 32.8%, 35%, 70%. Only 32.8% is in 26% to 34%.
